# SK5042 — A file or directory created writable by every local user

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

`UnixFileMode.OtherWrite` without the sticky bit lets any local process replace the contents of what this call creates.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Security |
| Default severity | error |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | no |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |
| Supersedes | S2612 |

## Why

World-writable means what it says: every account on the machine, including whatever a compromised unrelated service runs as, may overwrite the file. The damage is rarely the write itself — it is that this program will read the file back later and act on it, so a configuration file, a cache, a lock file or a script becomes an input an unprivileged local attacker controls. It is the kind of defect that never shows up in testing, because the developer's machine has one user and the container has one process. Drop `OtherWrite`; the owner and, where something genuinely shares, the group are what the bits are for. If this really is a shared drop directory where anyone may add an entry, say so by adding `UnixFileMode.StickyBit` — that is mode `1777`, what `/tmp` itself is, and it stops one user deleting or replacing another's entries. ⚠ There is no fix. Removing the bit is a one-token edit, but whether the remaining permissions are the ones this program actually needs depends on who else reads the file — a deployment fact the compiler cannot see, and a bit removed that something downstream depended on breaks at run time rather than at build time.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
File.SetUnixFileMode(
    path,
    UnixFileMode.UserRead | UnixFileMode.UserWrite | UnixFileMode.OtherRead | UnixFileMode.OtherWrite
);
```

Write:

```csharp
File.SetUnixFileMode(path, UnixFileMode.UserRead | UnixFileMode.UserWrite);
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **Issue #145 bundled three SonarQube rules and two of the three are refuted by measurement; this is the third, narrowed to the one bit that needs no judgement.** ⚠ **"A temporary file is created in a publicly writable directory" (`S5443`) is not decidable from the source, because the directory is not publicly writable on two of the three platforms.** Measured: `Path.GetTempPath()` returns a *per-user* directory on macOS — `/var/folders/…/T/`, mode `0700` — and `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Temp` on Windows. Only on Linux with `TMPDIR` unset is it `/tmp`. The same source text is a vulnerability or not depending on the machine it runs on, which makes it a property of the deployment rather than of the code. ⚠ **"Insecure temporary file creation methods" (`S5445`) is refuted on .NET.** Measured: `Path.GetTempFileName()` creates the file at mode `0600` — .NET goes through `mkstemp`, so the file exists, owned and private, before the name is returned, and the create-then-open race the rule is written about does not arise. What is left is a name-exhaustion limit at 65 535 files on Windows, which is a robustness bug and not a vulnerability. ⚠ **World-*readable* is not a rule either, for a measured reason**: plain `File.WriteAllText` creates at `0644`, so every ordinary file .NET writes is already world-readable because that is what the process umask says, and a rule reporting it would report every file-writing call in existence. This rule is about `OtherWrite` alone. ⚠ **`CA1416` is not this diagnostic and does not host it.** All three mode-setting APIs are `[UnsupportedOSPlatform("windows")]`, so `CA1416` — on by default at `warning` — does fire at an unscoped call site; but it fires on the *platform*, not the permission, and says exactly the same thing about `UnixFileMode.UserRead`, which is safe. The two are independent and measurably so: scoping the call site with `[SupportedOSPlatform("linux")]` or an `OperatingSystem.IsLinux()` guard silences `CA1416` completely and leaves `OtherWrite` reported by **nothing at all**, even under `AnalysisMode=All` with every `CA` raised. That residue — platform-scoped Unix code, which is the code that legitimately uses these APIs — is this rule's whole population. ⚠ **The sticky bit is the escape and it is the only one.** `OtherWrite` together with `StickyBit` is the shared drop-box idiom and the rule declines it. ⚠ **Only a compile-time-constant mode**, decided on the value the compiler already folded, so a mode assembled at run time out of variables is silence rather than a guess — whether it ends up world-writable is a question about another method. ⚠ **No receiver is named**: the rule matches on the *type* of the value, `System.IO.UnixFileMode`, wherever it is passed or assigned, which the BCL exposes at exactly four entry points today — `File.SetUnixFileMode(string, …)`, `File.SetUnixFileMode(SafeFileHandle, …)`, `Directory.CreateDirectory(string, UnixFileMode)` and the `FileStreamOptions.UnixCreateMode` property, a `UnixFileMode?`. None is written down, so a fifth arrives covered. ⚠ `File.Open` and `File.OpenHandle` take no mode at all; an earlier draft of this note said they did, and enumerating the BCL by reflection is what corrected it — the argument `SK5007` makes for certificate callbacks. ⚠ **Test methods are exempt**, by the attribute test six other rules already use: a test that creates a world-writable file in order to assert something about permissions is real, and a security rule at `error` that breaks a test suite teaches a reviewer to skim past every security finding. ⚠ **The reference trees prove nothing here and the zero is reported as such**: the shape occurs zero times in either tree, so the corpus zero is *shape absent* rather than *correctly declined*, and the evidence for this rule is its fixtures plus the sabotage set.
